entities.summary:
Antiochus VII Sidetes (antiochus-vii-sidetes) was the last Seleucid king of any stature, ruling from July/August 138 to 129 BC in the Hellenistic Seleucid Empire spanning from modern-day Turkey to Egypt. Born into a Hellenistic world, Antiochus VII Sidetes was a member of the Seleucid dynasty, which emerged from the vast territorial holdings of Alexander the Great, and was known for his long reign.

Antiochus VII Sidetes was nicknamed Sidetes, also known as Antiochus the Pious, and was a key figure in the struggle for control of the Seleucid Empire against his brother Seleucus VI Epiphanes, who would eventually succeed him. The empire's decline into fragmentation and the rise of the Parthian Empire marked the end of the Hellenistic period and had significant repercussions for the ancient world.

The reign of Antiochus VII Sidetes is notable for the Siege of Thapsus, where he clashed with the Roman general Scipio Aemilianus, leading to the eventual destruction of Carthage and the loss of the Seleucid Empire's territories in North Africa. This marked a significant turning point in the rise of Rome as a dominant world power.


The legacy of Antiochus VII Sidetes is one of a ruler who struggled to maintain the empire's territorial integrity in the face of internal strife and external pressures. His long reign and the empire's subsequent fragmentation have made him a subject of interest for historians studying the decline of the Hellenistic period and the rise of the Roman Empire.

Antiochus VII Sidetes (antiochus-vii-sidetes) played a pivotal role in the 1st Punic War, contributing to the eventual destruction of Carthage and the loss of the Seleucid Empire's territories in North Africa.

The reign of Antiochus VII Sidetes was marked by a series of military campaigns, including the conquest of Egypt, which he claimed as his own, and the Siege of Thapsus, where he clashed with the Roman general Scipio Aemilianus.
